bull.b: Strong demand across VEVYE and TRIESENCE shows that Harrow is expanding prescription adoption and commercial reach in multiple ophthalmic niches. Rising prescriptions, prescriber growth, market share, and surgical utilization support a durable revenue base beyond a single product or temporary launch effect.

The shift to positive operating and free cash flow improves Harrow’s ability to fund commercialization, support liquidity, and reduce reliance on external financing. Although cash flow remains modest relative to debt, sustained generation would strengthen financial resilience and provide flexibility for portfolio investment.

bull.t: Broader Dry-Eye Portfolio and Market Access
bull.b: Adding TYRVAYA gives Harrow a complementary dry-eye therapy and the opportunity to offer multiple branded options to physicians. Expanded PBM coverage can enlarge the addressable patient pool, improve access, and reinforce the company’s position across a strategically important ophthalmic category.

bear.t: Elevated Leverage and Thin Equity Cushion
bear.b: Higher leverage and a much smaller equity base reduce Harrow’s financial flexibility if operating performance weakens or acquisition spending rises. Debt-funded growth can increase refinancing pressure and constrain capital allocation, while the thin cushion leaves less protection against execution setbacks or additional losses.

bear.t: Persistent Losses and High Operating Costs
bear.b: High gross margins have not yet translated into consistent profitability, indicating that operating costs and other headwinds are absorbing much of the product-level economics. Continued losses limit internally generated capital, increase dependence on successful growth execution, and make earnings improvement a central business requirement.

The loss of pass-through reimbursement removes an important route to adoption for IHEEZO in ambulatory surgery centers and can limit utilization in a meaningful care setting. Harrow’s pivot toward in-office markets may offset some pressure, but reimbursement changes remain a structural constraint on product expansion.
